title: Fission-fragment rocket with direct conversion of fragment momentum into thrust

concept.text: A fission-fragment rocket would produce thrust by letting the fast, electrically charged products of nuclear fission escape from its fuel and directing their momentum into an exhaust beam. Conventional nuclear thermal propulsion first heats a propellant gas; this concept instead uses the fission products themselves as exhaust. Magnetic fields would redirect the initially scattered fragment trajectories so that their combined momentum pushes the spacecraft in a useful direction.

The fuel must expose fragments to very little material before they escape. Proposed arrangements include very thin fuel layers, small fuel particles in a dusty plasma, and aerogel-supported fuel. Local fuel thickness and the overall density of the assembly are separate design variables: small particles can permit escape, while the arrangement of the whole assembly determines neutron retention and useful fission power. A critical reactor must sustain its own chain reaction; an externally driven subcritical assembly would instead rely on a neutron source and neutron multiplication.

Neutral gas could also be introduced into the fragment stream to increase exhaust mass flow and thrust at the expense of specific impulse. This augmented mode overlaps with thermal propulsion because fragment energy is transferred to additional propellant. The defining advance remains the extraction and useful direction of fission fragments; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate an integrated engine achieving that advance.

significance.text: The potential advance is an exhaust velocity far above conventional nuclear thermal propulsion without requiring a bulk propellant gas to reach the corresponding temperature. Gahl and colleagues describe fission fragments carrying about 160 MeV in total and reaching speeds up to 5% of light speed, with conceptual engine specific impulses in the tens to hundreds of thousands of seconds. Fragment speed is a physical starting point, however, rather than a measurement of delivered engine performance: escape losses, exhaust directionality and the engine configuration determine how much becomes useful propulsion.

For a specified mission velocity change, sufficiently high effective specific impulse would substantially reduce propellant requirements. Fast outer-planet probes, cargo transport and interstellar precursor missions are plausible downstream possibilities if the engine also provides adequate thrust, sustained operation and manageable system mass. Propellant does not simply cease to dominate for every mission: the required velocity change still matters, and high exhaust velocity alone does not establish useful acceleration or short travel time. The proposed 10,000-second demonstration milestone would therefore establish an enabling capability, not those mission outcomes.

System mass is a consequential limit. Gahl discusses an early conceptual engine exceeding 113 metric tons and explains how its unexpended mass would limit final velocity. Reactor hardware, magnetic systems and thermal management must therefore be evaluated alongside exhaust performance. The projected neutral-gas mode offers a different thrust–specific-impulse tradeoff, but the cited calculations concern in-space propulsion and do not establish Earth-launch capability for the massive spacecraft considered. Nor do these sources assign crewed transport exclusively to either direct-fragment or gas-core thermal engines.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is an integrated fissile assembly that generates useful fission power, releases a substantial fraction of its fragments, directs them into an exhaust and produces measured net thrust. For a critical dusty-plasma design, the assembly must retain enough neutrons to sustain a chain reaction while allowing fragments to escape. This favors thin fuel and a low-density assembly spread over a large volume, creating a difficult geometry and neutron-utilization problem. An externally driven subcritical design need not reach criticality, but its feasibility instead depends on neutron-source performance, multiplication and the resulting system power balance.

Geometry is only one barrier. Puri and colleagues identify the containment of substantial fuel quantities at submicron scales and the establishment of a thrust axis from isotropically emitted particles as major challenges. Magnetic transport must be integrated with fuel containment and directional extraction, rather than demonstrated only with particles from a separate source. The proposed aerogel fuel arrangement also lacks an established path to criticality in the supplied experimental paper.

The integrated system must also close its power and heat balances and avoid excessive engine mass. Fragments that fail to escape deposit energy in the fuel or surrounding material instead of supplying the intended exhaust momentum. Useful operation consequently requires compatible fragment escape, fuel stability, thermal management and magnetic hardware over a meaningful operating duration. Solving neutron transport alone would leave these propulsion and engineering questions open.

current_state.text: Gahl, Gillespie, Duncan and Lin’s perspective, published on 13 October 2023, traces George Chapline’s thin-fuel fission-fragment propulsion concept to the late 1980s, including micron-thick fuel layers. It reports conceptual study values of 527,000 seconds specific impulse without added neutral gas and nearly 4.5 kN of thrust at 32,000 seconds with gas augmentation. These are calculated design results reported in a perspective, not measured engine performance. At its publication date, the article stated that no dusty-plasma reactor had been built or tested on Earth or in space.

The supplied later experiment is Sandeep Puri and colleagues’ Scientific Reports paper, published on 1 July 2025 as volume 15, article 22208. The researchers measured americium-241 alpha-particle detection and transport in a commercial 3-tesla Siemens MRI superconducting magnet, using alpha particles as surrogates for fission fragments. This demonstrates relevant detector and charged-particle transport work. It does not demonstrate a fissile propulsion assembly, direct fission-fragment exhaust or measured engine thrust.

The 2025 paper explicitly leaves open whether its proposed aerogel fuel assembly could be brought into a critical configuration. Alpha-surrogate measurements therefore do not resolve reactor criticality or the integration of fragment production, escape and thrust. The supplied review reports complete main-text access to both principal articles despite cookie-related redirects in the Nature retrieval. It did not visually inspect the experimental figures; the classification of the experiment rests on its explicit methods and conclusions.

Evidence-scope limitation: the supplied material contains no bounded search record establishing comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026. It supports the dated 2023 account and the specific 2025 experiment, but cannot establish that all subsequent work remains component science or that an integrated demonstration is absent worldwide at that later date. This coverage gap does not invalidate either documented result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: operate a low-density fissile assembly, either critical or externally driven subcritical, that produces a directed fission-fragment exhaust with independently measured net thrust, effective specific impulse above 10,000 seconds and a reported fragment-escape fraction. The 10,000-second threshold is an author-proposed milestone, not an established standard or a demonstrated result. For context, Gahl cites approximately 900 seconds for conventional nuclear thermal propulsion; that comparison does not establish a ceiling for every advanced thermal concept.
completion_criteria.label: Fission-fragment thrust demonstrates effective specific impulse above 10,000 seconds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirements: report operating duration, fission power, exhaust angular distribution, fragment-escape fraction and measurement uncertainties. State exactly which expelled masses enter the effective-specific-impulse calculation, including added gas where applicable. Demonstrate that measured force is attributable to the intended directed exhaust, with enough diagnostic information to connect thrust to fragment production and transport. Neutron-transport calculations or magnetic particle trajectories alone would not satisfy this propulsion milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Reported diagnostics establish thrust attribution and effective-specific-impulse mass accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed test setting: a contained ground experiment could qualify if it preserves the necessary vacuum and exhaust conditions and permits an interpretable thrust measurement; an in-space experiment could also qualify. A borehole should not be required or presumed suitable. The borehole discussion identified in the supplied review belongs to a separate nuclear thermal propulsion document concerning hydrogen-exhaust filtration, so it does not establish a facility solution for direct fragment exhaust.
completion_criteria.label: Experiment preserves vacuum and exhaust conditions enabling interpretable thrust measurements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed progression toward practical readiness: reproduce the result through repeated operation and independent verification, then characterize performance across relevant power levels, durations and fuel conditions. Report neutron-source requirements for subcritical operation, thermal loads, fuel containment and stability, and the mass of the complete propulsion system. Finite tests would establish demonstrated operating breadth, not universal capability. Mission readiness would require a separate showing that sustained thrust, lifetime and system mass support a specified spacecraft and trajectory.
completion_criteria.label: Independently verified repeated operation characterizes performance breadth and system requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—ROC-04, Open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket with high thrust and multi-thousand-second specific impulse: both concepts draw on fission energy, but their defining momentum pathways differ. A gas-core thermal rocket heats propellant, whereas ROC-05 seeks thrust directly from escaping fission products. Neutral-gas augmentation creates overlap by transferring fragment energy into additional propellant. Only ROC-04’s title is supplied, so its detailed performance, development barriers and suitability for crewed transport cannot be assessed here, and neither entry should be assigned exclusive ownership of crewed missions.

Roster synthesis—ROC-03, A directed-energy lightsail accelerated to a substantial fraction of light speed, and ROC-06, A plasma-magnet sail that takes useful delta-v from the solar wind: these share an interest in propulsion beyond ordinary chemical exhaust, but use different momentum sources. Their supplied titles identify an external light beam and the solar wind, respectively; ROC-05 would generate its exhaust momentum from onboard fission. Magnetic fields in a fragment engine would direct its own charged exhaust, a different role from coupling a plasma-magnet sail to the solar wind. These remain distinct concepts.

Roster synthesis—ROC-01, Sustained air-breathing combined-cycle flight to orbital speed, and ROC-02, Beamed-energy launch of a useful payload into orbit: these target ascent and orbital delivery. ROC-05 addresses a different propulsion opportunity centered on very high exhaust velocity for in-space use. Its conceptual performance figures do not demonstrate either air-breathing ascent or useful-payload launch from Earth, so it does not subsume those entries.

Roster synthesis—ROC-07, An operational momentum-exchange tether that moves payloads between orbits, and ROC-08, Industrial-scale production and loading of rocket propellant off Earth: these concern orbital momentum exchange and propellant infrastructure rather than direct fragment thrust. They could coexist with a fission-fragment transportation system, but reduced propellant requirements would not by themselves demonstrate either tether operations or off-Earth propellant production and loading.

Adjacent-concept qualification: thin-film radioisotope decay propulsion has a conceptual resemblance because emitted nuclear-decay products can carry momentum away from a surface. The research names NASA’s TFINER concept, but the supplied evidence does not establish that specific identification or its comparative thrust. Radioisotope decay propulsion should remain an adjacent idea rather than being treated as an achieved version of this fissile-assembly engine or merged into ROC-05.

change_log.reason: The research and review support a distinct propulsion concept whose mechanism needs to be understandable independently of its projected performance.

change_log.change: Separated local fuel thickness, bulk assembly density, critical operation and externally driven subcritical operation.
change_log.reason: Subcritical designs do not universally require critical geometry; their neutron-source requirements, multiplication and power balance are separate constraints.

change_log.change: Expanded the missing breakthrough beyond low-density critical geometry to include fuel containment, directional extraction, thermal management and system mass.
change_log.reason: The reviewed sources identify integration barriers that geometry alone does not capture.

change_log.change: Retained 527,000 seconds, nearly 4.5 kN and 32,000 seconds as conceptual study values, and added the supported fragment-energy, speed and early engine-mass context.
change_log.reason: These quantitative details explain both the attraction and the limitations without presenting calculations as experimental achievements.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that propellant mass almost stops dominating with a fixed-velocity-change benefit and conditional mission implications.
change_log.reason: Required velocity change, acceleration, operating life, power and dry mass determine whether high exhaust performance produces practical mission gains.

change_log.change: Dated the dusty-plasma no-test statement to 2023 and narrowed later experimental claims to the supplied July 2025 paper.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish worldwide absence of an integrated engine or comprehensive field coverage through November 2026.

change_log.change: Clarified the MRI experiment’s alpha-surrogate scope, unresolved aerogel criticality and lack of a thrust measurement.
change_log.reason: Particle detection and transport are meaningful component achievements but do not establish integrated fission-fragment propulsion.

change_log.reason: A proposed threshold needs explicit mass accounting, uncertainties and operating boundaries, and must not be mistaken for a consensus standard or mission qualification.

change_log.change: Explained all supplied roster relationships without merging entries, and qualified the TFINER comparison and exclusive assignment of crewed transport to ROC-04.
change_log.reason: The roster provides titles rather than detailed evidence for other entries, and the principal sources do not establish those broader comparisons.

change_log.change: Preserved the relevant review-access limitation and excluded unrelated or insufficiently reviewed artifacts from scientific support.
change_log.reason: Complete principal-article text supports the stated findings, but uninspected figures, a truncated software manual and ancillary documents should not imply additional verification.

unresolved_issues: Whether an integrated fission-fragment thrust demonstration occurred after the supplied dated studies remains unestablished; the supplied freshness record contains no bounded search coverage through 1 November 2026.
Whether an aerogel fuel assembly can achieve a useful critical configuration, or a subcritical configuration with acceptable neutron-source requirements and system power balance, remains unresolved.
No integrated measured values are supplied for fragment escape, exhaust directionality, thrust, effective specific impulse, operating life or complete propulsion-system mass.
The extent to which the alpha-surrogate experiment predicts actual fission-fragment extraction and direction in an operating fissile assembly remains a question for further demonstration.
A suitable contained ground-test arrangement, including any borehole implementation, has not been established by the supplied evidence.
The specific TFINER identification and lower-thrust comparison remain unverified; the conceptual adjacency is retained without asserting those details.
Only roster titles are supplied for the other innovations, limiting detailed comparisons of performance, readiness and mission suitability.

brief.title: Space travel powered by fragments of split atoms
possible: Spacecraft could carry less propellant for journeys that demand large changes in speed. An engine would use the fast, charged fragments released when atoms split as its exhaust, with magnetic fields steering them to push the spacecraft.
This could support faster probes to the outer planets, cargo transport and missions reaching beyond the Solar System.
why: Faster exhaust means less propellant is needed for a given change in spacecraft speed. Using the fragments directly would avoid having to heat a whole propellant gas to achieve that exhaust speed.

sources.who: J. Gahl, A. K. Gillespie, R. V. Duncan and C. Lin
sources.showed: Their perspective reviewed calculated engine designs that use escaping fragments for thrust. Adding gas to the exhaust increased predicted thrust while reducing propellant efficiency.
sources.quote: The study showed further that, without increasing the reactor power, adding a neutral gas to the fission fragment beam significantly increased the FFRE thrust.
sources.cited_for: The designs explain how fragment exhaust could provide high propellant efficiency and how added gas could increase thrust.
sources.not_established: Calculated performance does not establish that an operating engine can release and steer fragments to produce measured thrust.

sources.showed: They measured the detection and transport of alpha particles, charged particles used as stand-ins for fission fragments, inside a strong MRI magnet.
sources.quote: Our COMSOL simulations confirm that up to an ion current of ~ 300 A, these perturbations remain sufficiently small such that particle confinement and extraction—critical to propulsion and to experimental validation via scintillator detection—are not compromised.
sources.cited_for: The experiments support studying fragment-like particle transport in strong magnetic fields.
sources.not_established: They did not demonstrate actual fission-fragment exhaust, an operating nuclear fuel assembly or engine thrust.

shown: Gahl and colleagues reviewed calculated designs with high specific impulse: thrust divided by the weight of propellant expelled each second. These were design calculations, not measured engine performance.

Puri and colleagues tested particle detection and transport in an MRI magnet. Their alpha particles stood in for fission fragments; the experiment did not combine nuclear fuel, fragment escape and measured thrust.
missing: An integrated engine must generate nuclear power, let a substantial share of fragments escape, steer them and produce measured net thrust.
Fuel must let fragments escape while sustaining a chain reaction, or work with an external neutron source that fits the engine's power budget.
Fuel containment, heat removal and magnetic steering must work together for sustained operation without excessive engine mass.

milestones.label: Measured fragment thrust exceeds the proposed efficiency threshold
milestones.explanation: A low-density fuel assembly, self-sustaining or externally driven, would need independently measured thrust, specific impulse above 10,000 seconds and a reported escape fraction. This would demonstrate useful direct fragment propulsion.

milestones.label: Measurements connect thrust to fragments and account for expelled mass
milestones.explanation: Measurements would need duration, nuclear power, exhaust directions, escape fraction, uncertainties and all expelled mass, including added gas. These would establish the thrust's source and make its efficiency interpretable.

milestones.label: Test conditions permit interpretable thrust measurements
milestones.explanation: A contained ground test or a space test would need to preserve suitable vacuum and exhaust conditions. This would allow a meaningful thrust measurement.

milestones.label: Repeated operation establishes performance and whole-engine requirements
milestones.explanation: Repeated, independently verified tests would need to span power, duration and fuel conditions, measuring neutron-source needs, heat, fuel stability and containment, and total mass. This would establish the demonstrated operating range.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether fuel held in an extremely light aerogel structure can sustain a chain reaction or work efficiently with an external neutron source.
How well alpha-particle tests predict actual fragment escape and steering in operating nuclear fuel remains unresolved.
The efficiency threshold is proposed, not an established standard; mission readiness also depends on sustained thrust, lifetime and total engine mass.

page.title: Fission-fragment rocket engine
page.definition: A rocket engine produces thrust by letting the charged nuclei created when atoms split escape its fuel and magnetically directing them into an exhaust beam. The fission fragments themselves carry the exhaust momentum.

goal.need: Fission fragments carry about 160 MeV per fission and can reach 5% of light speed. Direct fragment exhaust uses this motion without first heating a bulk propellant. Specific impulse, the thrust impulse divided by expended propellant weight at Earth's gravity, quantifies the propellant-use advantage sought in the designs below.

completion.title: A fission-fragment engine produces measurable thrust from a magnetically directed fragment exhaust.
completion.criterion: An integrated fission-fragment system produces measurable net thrust by magnetically directing fragments escaping its nuclear fuel. The NIAC study roadmap specifies no minimum thrust, specific impulse, fission power or operating duration for this system demonstration.
completion.set_by: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center's NIAC study team, Proposed FFRE Roadmap, report page 37. The measurable-thrust target appears only in the figure and was written for the dusty-plasma architecture.
completion.basis: The study places measurable thrust after magnetic flow control and before later moderator and thermal integration. This is a published propulsion-demonstration target. Its scope is engine thrust from directed fission fragments; the roadmap leaves numerical acceptance limits unspecified.

milestones.title: An experiment controls the nuclear fuel in a fission-fragment core.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate nuclear fuel control experimentally. The roadmap supplies no inventory, power or retention-time requirement. The perspective published on 13 October 2023 describes micron-thick fuel coatings on carbon fibres for thin-layer engines; this is a proposed fuel arrangement rather than an operating-core demonstration.
milestones.set_by: NASA, 2015 Technology Roadmaps, TA 2, section 2.3.6, page TA 2-33.

milestones.title: Nuclear fuel in a fission-fragment core demonstrates self-cooling.
milestones.criterion: Experimentally demonstrate fuel self-cooling. The roadmap supplies no temperature, power or duration requirement. The perspective published on 13 October 2023 describes radiative cooling in proposed engines and states that no dusty-plasma reactor had been built or tested.
milestones.set_by: NASA, 2015 Technology Roadmaps, TA 2, section 2.3.6, page TA 2-33.

milestones.title: An experiment establishes fission-fragment escape efficiency from the engine's fuel.
milestones.criterion: Experimentally establish fragment escape efficiency; NASA specifies no minimum fraction. The manuscript posted on 13 March 2026 reports one 8.8 mg, 0.25 cm³ uranium-loaded graphene-aerogel sample irradiated with 14 MeV neutrons for 2 hours. A CR-39 plastic detector recorded 5,590 ± 475 fission-fragment tracks. The authors inferred the total escaping population using transport calculations; this establishes fragment escape with model-dependent efficiency estimates.
milestones.set_by: NASA, 2015 Technology Roadmaps, TA 2, section 2.3.6, page TA 2-33.

milestones.title: Magnetic fields direct escaping fission fragments into an exhaust beam.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate magnetic flow control of escaping fission fragments, the roadmap's system-demonstration step immediately before measurable thrust. No beam-divergence or extraction-efficiency limit is specified. The paper published on 1 July 2025 imaged particles from four americium-241 alpha sources in a 3 T MRI magnet. It demonstrated surrogate-particle transport; an exhaust beam of actual fission fragments was not tested.
milestones.set_by: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center's NIAC study team, Proposed FFRE Roadmap, report page 37. Magnetic flow control appears only in the figure, originally for dusty-plasma fuel.

not_found: No published integrated fission-fragment engine thrust measurement was found in NASA, NTRS, arXiv or journal searches through 14 November 2026.
No experimental acceptance protocol specifying minimum thrust, uncertainty or operating duration for direct fission-fragment propulsion was found.
The NASA and USRA copies of the 2015 propulsion roadmap could not be opened; its July 2015 final text was accessible through a Scribd mirror.
The publisher's full text of the 2026 aerogel study was inaccessible; its arXiv manuscript was accessible.

results.finding: A uranium oxide layer simulation, with no physical samples, estimated nearly 100% heavy-ion escape below a few microns.
results.detail: The result comes from a transport simulation, not an experimental measurement of fragment escape efficiency.
results.quote:
The results of the simulation, illustrated in
Figure 1
, confirm that nearly 100% of heavy ions can escape for layer thicknesses below a few microns.

results.finding: Four americium-241 sources produced an approximately 5.2-fold experimental increase in detected alpha particles.
results.detail: A 3 T magnetic field confined alpha particles used as fission-fragment surrogates. The experiment did not test an exhaust beam of actual fission fragments.
results.quote: However, with a 3-T magnetic field, there is a significant increase in the count of escaping particles—6.5 times (~ 5.2 times from experiment) at a distance of 20”, 4.0 times (~ 3.7 times from experiment) at 15”, and 2.0 times (~ 3.2 times from experiment) at 10”.

results.finding: One uranium-loaded graphene-aerogel sample produced 5,590 ± 475 recorded fission-fragment tracks.
results.detail: The 8.8 mg sample was irradiated with 14 MeV neutrons for two hours. The estimated escaping fraction was about 40%, based on transport calculations and an inferred total fragment population.
results.quote:
From 4.8×109 total 14 MeV neutrons incident, 5,590 ± 475 FF tracks were recorded in the 
CR-39.
